description:
We’re a multidisciplinary team taking on the Health Monitoring Software challenge. Our goal is software that keeps astronauts healthy on long missions to the Moon and Mars, where help from Earth can be many minutes away.

Who we are: software engineers, AI engineers, a lawyer, and a project management and documentation lead. We combine strong engineering with something most teams overlook: responsible handling of health data, including privacy, consent and ethics.
summary:
On a mission to Mars, help from Earth can be up to 22 minutes away, one way. The crew can’t wait for doctors on the ground to notice a health problem, so they need to spot changes early and act on their own.

Nova Healix is a web app that tracks the health of a four-person crew on a simulated 260-day trip to Mars. It is built around NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity, and a closed environment. Each astronaut gets a score from 0 to 100 for each hazard. The scores are based on that person’s own normal ranges, not an average.

The flight surgeon sees the whole crew, findings with the evidence behind them, and suggested actions. Astronauts do a short daily check-in and a camera balance test, and can talk to Nova, a private AI companion. Space weather and the Earth–Mars distance come from real NASA data.
details:
What it does
Nova Healix has two views. Mission Control is for the flight surgeon. It shows all four astronauts, their live vitals, and a 0–100 score for each of NASA’s five hazards. When something changes, the app creates a finding that says what changed, why it matters, the data behind it, and what to do next. The flight surgeon can act on a finding, resolve it, or reopen it, and every action is logged.

Crew Mode is for the astronaut. They see their own health in plain language, fill in a 30-second daily check-in, answer short questionnaires, and do a camera mobility and balance check. They can also talk to Nova, a private AI companion.

How it works
Every reading is compared with that astronaut’s own normal range. A heart rate that is fine for one person can be a warning sign for another. A score of 40 or more is marked Watch and 70 or more is marked Alert. These thresholds are our own and are only for the prototype, not for medical use.

Real NASA data

  • NASA DONKI: a real solar storm is replayed on mission Day 97 and drives the radiation dose.
  • NASA JPL Horizons: the real Earth–Mars distance sets the signal delay shown in the app.
  • NASA’s five hazards and NASA-STD-3001 guided how we set the scores and limits.

The crew data is simulated. No real astronaut data was used.

Privacy
Health data is personal, so we kept it private by default. Nova conversations stay on the astronaut’s device and Mission Control never sees them. The only exception is safety: if an astronaut describes a risk of serious harm or an urgent medical problem, the flight surgeon gets an alert. The alert says help is needed but never shows what was written, and Nova tells the astronaut when it sends one. The camera check runs in the browser and the video never leaves the device.

Why it matters
Long missions will need crews to look after their own health with little help from Earth. The same idea could also help in remote clinics, polar research stations, and home care.

What we used
Angular and TypeScript for the frontend, hosted on Vercel. FastAPI on Railway for the backend, with Supabase for storage. MediaPipe Pose for the camera check, and Google Gemini for Nova’s replies (safety replies are pre-written, not generated). Apache ECharts for charts.

Use of AI
We used AI coding help (Claude) to build the frontend, and Google Gemini writes Nova’s replies inside the app. Our team planned the product, designed the screens and flows, and reviewed and tested the code.
